'''''Typha angustifolia''''' is a [[perennial]] [[herbaceous plant|herbaceous]] plant in the genus ''[[Typha]]'', [[native plant|native]] throughout most of [[Eurasia]] and locally in northwest [[Africa]]; it also occurs widely in [[North America]], where its native status is disputed. It is an "obligate wetland" species that is found in fresh water or [[Brackish water|brackish]] locations. It is known in [[British English]] as '''lesser bulrush''',<ref name=BSBI_Atlas2020>{{cite web |title=Lesser Bulrush ''Typha angustifolia'' L. |work=BSBI Online Plant Atlas 2020 |editor1=P.A. Stroh |editor2=T. A. Humphrey |editor3=R.J. Burkmar |editor4=O.L. Pescott |editor5=D.B. Roy |editor6=K.J. Walker |publisher=Botanical Society of Britain and Ireland |date=2020 |url=https://plantatlas2020.org/atlas/2cd4p9h.25e |access-date=21 October 2024 }}</ref><ref name = "Streeter">Streeter D, Hart-Davies C, Hardcastle A, Cole F, Harper L. 2009. ''Collins Flower Guide''. Harper Collins {{ISBN|9-78-000718389-0}}</ref><ref name=Wild_Flower_Web>{{cite web |title=Lesser Bulrush |work=Wild Flower Web |author=Aaron Kitching |url=http://www.wildflowerweb.co.uk/plant/1538/lesser-bulrush |access-date=15 June 2024 }}</ref> and in [[North American English]] as '''narrowleaf cattail'''.<ref name=USDA>{{PLANTS|id=TYAN|taxon=Typha angustifolia|access-date=12 December 2015}}</ref>

== Description ==
''Typha angustifolia'' grows {{Convert|1.5|–|2|m}} high (rarely to 3 m) and has slender [[leaves]] {{Convert|3–12|mm|abbr=on}} broad, obviously slenderer than in the related ''[[Typha latifolia]]''; ten or fewer leaves arise from each vegetative shoot. The leaves are deciduous, appearing in spring and dying down in the autumn.<ref name = "Streeter"/><ref name=blamey>Blamey, M. & Grey-Wilson, C. (1989). ''Flora of Britain and Northern Europe''. {{ISBN|0-340-40170-2}}</ref><ref name=CABI>{{citation | last=Murphy | first=Kevin | title=Typha angustifolia (lesser bulrush) | publisher=CABI Publishing | date=2022-01-07 | doi=10.1079/cabicompendium.54294 | doi-access=free | page=}}</ref> The flowering stem is {{Convert|1|–|1.5|m}} tall, distinctly shorter than the leaves and hidden among them, unlike ''Typha latifolia'' where the flowering stem is as tall as or taller than the leaves. The flowers form in a dense cluster at the top of the main stem; they are divided into a female portion below, and a tassel of male flowers above; the female and male parts are separated by a gap of {{Convert|3|–|8|cm}} (rarely to 12 cm) of bare stem, which distinguishes the species readily from ''Typha latifolia'' where there is no gap between the female and male flowers.<ref name = "Streeter"/><ref name=blamey/> Flowering is in June to July; after this, the male portion falls off, leaving the female portion to form a rusty-brown fruit head 13–25 mm diameter, maturing into the familiar sausage-shaped spike. The gap between the female and male flowers remains visible as a smooth part at the base of the spike that held the male flowers. The seed heads persist through the winter, and then gradually break up in spring to release the tiny seeds embedded in hairs which assist with wind dispersal.<ref name = "Streeter"/><ref name=CABI/><ref name=FoEA>{{cite web | title=Bulrushes | website=Flora of East Anglia | url=http://webidguides.com/_templates/group_typha.html | access-date=2024-10-22}}</ref> The plants have sturdy, [[rhizomatous]] roots that can extend {{Convert|70|cm}} and are typically {{Convert|2|-|4|cm}} diameter.<ref name=CABI/>

== Distribution ==
[[File:Typha angustifolia (habitus) 1.jpg|thumb|left|''Typha angustifolia'', mature fruiting stems, Volgograd Reservoir, Russia]]
The species is universally accepted to be native across most of Eurasia, and in the far northwest of Africa, where it is widely distributed in temperate and subtropical regions, growing in marshes, wetlands, and along the edges of ponds and lakes.<ref name=POWO/> Its status in North America, accepted as native by some,<ref name=POWO/> remains far from clear. In 1987 it was argued that the species was introduced from Europe to North America, with a human-mediated arrival on the east coast between 1800–1820.<ref name=Stuckey>{{cite journal|last1=Stuckey|first1=R. L.|last2=Salamon|first2=D. P.|year=1987|title=''Typha angustifolia'' in North America: masquerading as a native| url=https://kb.osu.edu/server/api/core/bitstreams/50e3c1d3-eb53-52d9-9683-7075d3a35a41/content | journal=Ohio Journal of Science| volume=87| page=4| access-date=2024-10-22}}</ref> Later, pollen data gave credence to the idea that the species was present in North America pre-contact,<ref>{{cite journal | doi=10.1672/07-40.1 | title=Range dynamics and invasive tendencies in Typha latifolia and Typha angustifolia in eastern North America derived from herbarium and pollen records | date=2008 | last1=Shih | first1=Jessica G. | last2=Finkelstein | first2=Sarah A. | journal=Wetlands | volume=28 | issue=1 | pages=1–16 | bibcode=2008Wetl...28....1S }}</ref> but subsequent examination of this question suggests it remains very uncertain: "''T. angustifolia'' is likely not native with European origins", with the species no more than "possibly native to the tidal wetlands of the eastern seaboard".<ref name=Bansal>{{cite journal |display-authors=et al | last1=Bansal | first1=Sheel | title=Typha (Cattail) Invasion in North American Wetlands: Biology, Regional Problems, Impacts, Ecosystem Services, and Management | journal=Wetlands | publisher=Springer Science and Business Media LLC | volume=39 | issue=4 | date=2019-06-21 | issn=0277-5212 | doi=10.1007/s13157-019-01174-7 | doi-access=free | pages=645–684| hdl=20.500.12648/2228 | hdl-access=free }}</ref> Within North America, it is also thought to have spread recently from coastal to inland locations.<ref>{{cite journal|last=Mills|first=Edward L.|author2=Leach, Joseph H.|author3=Carlton, James T.|author4=Secor, Carol L.|year=1993|title=Exotic Species in the Great Lakes: A History of Biotic Crises and Anthropogenic Introductions|url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/222450832|journal=Journal of Great Lakes Research|volume=19|issue=1|doi=10.1016/S0380-1330(93)71197-1|bibcode=1993JGLR...19....1M |access-date=2013-10-21|page=46|quote=The distributional history of the narrow-leaved cattail, a brackish water species native to the Atlantic coast, is debatable. It began a rapid inland expansion in through Central New York in the first half of the 20th Century when the de-icing of highways using salt became more widespread.|doi-access=free}}</ref>

The geographic range of ''Typha angustifolia'' overlaps with the very similar species ''[[Typha latifolia]]''. ''T. angustifolia'' can be distinguished from ''T. latifolia'' by its narrower leaves and by a clear separation of two different regions (staminate flowers above and pistilate flowers below) on the flowering heads.<ref name="Streeter"/> ''T. angustifolia'' often occurs in deeper water than ''T. latifolia'', and is more tolerant of wetlands with low [[eutrophication]] conditions.<ref name="Streeter"/><ref name=BSBI_Atlas2020/>

The two species can produce [[hybrid (biology)|hybrids]], named as ''Typha × glauca'' (''Typha angustifolia x T. latifolia''); it is a sterile [[F1 hybrid]], which reproduces only vegetatively, forming [[clonal colony|clonal colonies]], which may be extensive.<ref name=BSBI_Atlas2020_2>{{cite web |title=''Typha angustifolia × latifolia'' = ''T. × ⁠glauca'' Godr. |work=BSBI Online Plant Atlas 2020 |editor1=P.A. Stroh |editor2=T. A. Humphrey |editor3=R.J. Burkmar |editor4=O.L. Pescott |editor5=D.B. Roy |editor6=K.J. Walker |publisher=Botanical Society of Britain and Ireland |date=2020 |url=https://plantatlas2020.org/atlas/2cd4p9h.pve |access-date=21 October 2024 }}</ref>

==Culinary use==
{{See also|Typha latifolia#Uses}}
Several parts of the plant are edible, including during various seasons the dormant sprouts on roots and bases of leaves, the inner core of the stalk, green bloom spikes, ripe pollen, and starchy roots.<ref>{{cite book |last1= Elias |first1= Thomas S. |last2=Dykeman |first2=Peter A. |title= Edible Wild Plants |year=2009 |orig-date= 1982 |publisher=Sterling Publishing Co., Inc. |location=New York, NY |isbn=978-1-4027-6715-9 |pages=69–70 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=Typha angustifolia - Small reed mace|url=http://www.pfaf.org/user/Plant.aspx?LatinName=Typha%20angustifolia|access-date=2011-03-16|website=Plants for a Future}}</ref> It can be prepared in the same way as ''Typha latifolia''.<ref name=":0">{{Cite book|last1=Elias|first1=Thomas S.|title=Edible Wild Plants: A North American Field Guide to Over 200 Natural Foods|last2=Dykeman|first2=Peter A.|publisher=[[Sterling Publishing|Sterling]]|year=2009|isbn=978-1-4027-6715-9|location=New York|page=69|oclc=244766414|orig-date=1982}}</ref> The edible stem is called {{Lang|vi|bồn bồn}} in Vietnam.<sup>[https://www.flickr.com/photos/vietnamfriendly/699040225/ photo]</sup>
